raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old boy was referred to our hospital for persistent fever, cough and weight loss for 3 weeks duration. He had previously consulted in a peripheral hospital where a chest X-ray was normal and a treatment for acute bronchitis was prescribed (thiamphenicol and clavulanic acid and amoxicillin).
On admission, he was conscious but in respiratory distress, with dyspnoea, and polypnea of 56 cycles/min, the heart rate was 108beats/min and temperature of 38.7 C. He presented a hepatomegaly, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds. He was admitted in the paediatric intensive care unit. A thoracoabdominal sonogram showed a left liver lobe abscess. A chest and abdominal computer tomography scan (CT scan) was requested to further characterize the liver abscess. It showed bilateral pleuropneumopathy, a diaphragmatic collection thru the larrey's aperture, hepatosplenomegaly, and minor ascites [Figures 1-4]. The amoebic serology was normal. He was placed on IV antibiotic (amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, and gentamicin). A review of the scan films made us suspect a pericardial effusion or amediastinal abscess. A rightmediastinal drainage was done and evacuated 500ml of frank greenish pus. There was no improvement with that regimen. The antibiotic was changed to ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/24 h, metronidazole (mg/kg/24 h) and gentamicin (5 mg/kg/24 h). The child was further stabilized with a blood transfusion for severe anaemia. The evolution was marked by no improvement after 3 days and he was more ill, the preoperative American Society of Anesthesia (ASA) was in class V. He then underwent a thoracotomy and a pericardiectomy at day 4 from admission. Twolitres of frank pus were removed from the pericardium. Two drains were left in place. AT J3 after the surgery, he remained febrile, the culture of the pus growed Staphylococcus aureus, and the HIV serology requested after counselling of the mother was positive. Based on the antibiogram, gentamicin was stopped and ciprofloxacin was started. At J9 post-operatively the temperature subsided and the hemodynamic parameters improved, but there was a persistent purulent drainage. AT J13, he was stable, a corticotherapy was introduced to decrease the fibrosis and drains were removed. The chest radiograph showed a persistent bilateral lower lobe infiltrate and a mild cardiomegaly. The cardiac sonogram showed a thickened pericardium, but no pericardial effusion and no valvular anomaly. AT J24, he was discharged home with per os ciprofloxacin and iron treatment. The steroids were stopped. He was seen in the out-patient department 1 week after and was doing well. He was again seen 1 month after discharged. The confirmation HIV testing was still positive, the Cluster determination (Lymphocytes T4) [CD4] count was 14 cells/ml. He was placed on antiretroviral drugs associated to cotrimoxazole. The child was referred back to his hospital were the mother was a nurse. After counselling, the mother admitted being on antiretroviral treatment for many years.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old boy was referred with a 3-week history of persistent fever, cough, and weight loss, presenting in acute respiratory distress.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 3 weeks prior to referral, the child experienced persistent fever, cough, and weight loss that failed to improve after outpatient treatment for presumed acute bronchitis (thiamphenicol and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, with a normal initial chest X-ray) at a peripheral hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable prior medical history reported at admission; post-diagnosis counseling revealed that his mother (a nurse) was HIV-positive and had been on antiretroviral therapy for many years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 3-week fever, cough, weight loss, and acute dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: On admission to the PICU, the child was conscious but in severe respiratory distress with tachypnea (56 breaths/min), tachycardia (108 beats/min), and fever (38.7 °C). Cardiovascular and abdominal examination revealed jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, and hepatomegaly (ASA physical status class V prior to thoracotomy).
objective.routine_investigations: Severe anemia requiring packed red blood cell transfusion; negative amoebic serology; positive HIV serology (confirmed 1 month post-discharge). Pericardial/mediastinal pus culture grew Staphylococcus aureus. Postoperative day 13 chest X-ray showed persistent bilateral lower lobe infiltrates and mild cardiomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count at 1-month post-discharge follow-up was 14 cells/mL. Thoracoabdominal ultrasound and thoracoabdominal CT demonstrated a left hepatic lobe abscess, bilateral pleuropneumonia, an anterior diaphragmatic/mediastinal collection extending through Larrey's space, massive purulent pericarditis, hepatosplenomegaly, and mild ascites. Initial right mediastinal drainage evacuated 500 mL of frank greenish pus, and day 4 open thoracotomy and pericardiectomy evacuated 2,000 mL of frank pericardial pus. Postoperative day 13 echocardiogram showed pericardial thickening without residual effusion or valvular abnormality.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Staphylococcus aureus left hepatic lobe abscess complicated by transdiaphragmatic rupture through Larrey's space causing anterior mediastinal abscess and massive purulent pericarditis with cardiac tamponade, unmasking vertically acquired pediatric HIV/AIDS (confirmed by repeat positive HIV serology and CD4+ T-cell count of 14 cells/mL). Managed with initial mediastinal drainage (500 mL pus), day 4 open thoracotomy and pericardiectomy (2 L pus evacuated), blood transfusion, short-course adjunctive corticosteroids (started day 13 to prevent constrictive pericardial fibrosis), and targeted antimicrobial therapy switched from amoxicillin-clavulanate/gentamicin and ceftriaxone/metronidazole/gentamicin to ciprofloxacin based on S. aureus susceptibility. Discharged on postoperative day 24 on oral ciprofloxacin and iron supplementation, and subsequently initiated on antiretroviral therapy and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis at 1-month follow-up.
